name: french quiche
instructions:
A french-leaning quiche adapted from a standard american ham-and-cheese-quiche article recipe. Cheese + mushrooms + parsley + nutmeg + Julia-Child-ratio custard in a pie crust. Standard 9-inch pie plate format.

CUSTARD RATIO (Julia Child): 3 eggs to 1.5 cups liquid (milk or cream). Scale up proportionally as needed for a full 9-inch quiche — commonly 4-5 eggs with 2-2.5 cups liquid works well. The article version used 6 eggs to 3/4 cup dairy, which came out eggy (see notes) — Julia's ratio is the corrected version.

INGREDIENTS (one 9-inch quiche):
- 1 single unbaked pie crust (see savory-pie-crust for the from-scratch version; store-bought works too)
- eggs + milk/cream at Julia Child's ratio (3 eggs : 1.5 cups liquid; scale as needed)
- 3/4 tsp salt
- 1/4 tsp black pepper
- ~1 cup cooked mushrooms (see notes on prep — must be dry, not wet)
- 1 1/2 cups shredded gruyere or monterrey jack cheese, divided (1 cup in the base, 1/2 cup on top) — both work, see cheese note
- 3 tbsp finely chopped fresh parsley
- freshly grated nutmeg for dusting the top

PROCEDURE:
1. Preheat oven to 375°F.
2. Unroll the pie crust and press it into a 9-inch pie plate, crimping the top edges.
3. PREP THE MUSHROOMS: slice, sauté in a little butter or oil until soft AND until the released liquid has fully evaporated (moisture control is load-bearing here — see notes). Set aside to cool briefly.
4. In a large bowl, whisk together eggs, milk (or cream), salt, and pepper at the Julia Child ratio.
5. Scatter the cooked-and-dried mushrooms, 1 cup of the shredded cheese, and the chopped parsley evenly across the crust.
6. Pour the egg mixture over top.
7. Sprinkle the remaining 1/2 cup cheese on top of the egg mixture.
8. DUST THE TOP WITH FRESHLY GRATED NUTMEG — see notes on why this move works.
9. Bake 35-40 min until the center is completely set (a slight jiggle in the middle is fine; it'll finish setting as it rests).
10. Let cool 5-10 min before slicing and serving.
notes:
=== SOURCE + WHAT THE RECIPE IS NOW ===

Adapted from a standard american ham-and-cheese quiche article recipe. Iterations have moved it further from the article and closer to a classical french quiche:
- CHEESE: gruyere OR monterrey jack (article used cheddar). Both work — see cheese note.
- PROTEIN / VEGETABLE: cooked mushrooms (article used ham). Meat-forward → vegetable-forward.
- HERB: parsley (article used green onions). Quieter, more french-neutral.
- FINISH: nutmeg dusted on top before baking (not in article). Classical french move — see nutmeg note.
- CUSTARD RATIO: Julia Child's 3 eggs : 1.5 cups liquid (article used 6 eggs : 3/4 cup — too egg-heavy, see ratio note).

=== CHEESE — GRUYERE OR MONTERREY JACK, BOTH WORK ===

Gruyere is the classical french quiche cheese — nutty, sharp, alpine, and the traditional pick for something like a quiche lorraine. Monterrey jack is the everyday-fridge substitute that gets closer than cheddar would; melts mildly, doesn't dominate the egg base. Reach for whichever is around. Nutmeg + cheese (either one) stays as the core flavor stack.

=== NUTMEG ON TOP — THE 'MAKES IT TASTE MORE EXPENSIVE' MOVE ===

Dust the top with freshly grated nutmeg before baking. This is the single most under-appreciated move in the whole recipe. Nutmeg on cream-based egg dishes is a classical french technique (also see: bechamel, gratin dauphinois) — a background warm-spice depth that ties dairy + egg together and reads distinctly french.

FRESH-GRATED IS BETTER THAN PRE-GROUND: pre-ground nutmeg loses its volatile oils fast and reads flat. A whole nutmeg + microplane sitting in the spice cabinet is a real quality-per-dollar upgrade. If you only have pre-ground, use it, but plan to upgrade eventually.

Don't overdo — a few passes of the microplane across the top is enough. The goal is a background elevator, not a distinctive nutmeg flavor.

=== JULIA CHILD'S CUSTARD RATIO — 3 EGGS : 1.5 CUPS LIQUID ===

Julia Child's classical quiche custard ratio is 3 eggs to 1.5 cups of liquid (milk or cream). This is the right ratio for a proper french quiche — silky custard, not eggy scramble.

The original article's ratio (6 eggs to 3/4 cup dairy) is way off in the other direction — twice as many eggs to a fifth as much liquid, roughly. Confirmed empirically on the first cook: reads as a baked-omelette-in-a-crust, not a silky custard. Julia's ratio corrects this.

Scaling for a full 9-inch quiche: 4-5 eggs with 2-2.5 cups liquid is a common scale-up (same ratio, more volume) that fills the pie plate properly. Adjust based on how deep the crust is.

=== MOISTURE CONTROL IS LOAD-BEARING (SAME LOGIC AS THE FRITTATA) ===

MUSHROOMS MUST BE COOKED AND DRY BEFORE THEY GO IN: mushrooms release a lot of water when they cook. If you put raw mushrooms into the quiche, the water they release ends up in the custard and the middle stays wet while the edges over-bake. Sauté the mushrooms in a little butter or oil until softened AND until all the released liquid has fully evaporated — then they're safe to add. Same rule as tomatoes/zucchini in the marcella frittata.

=== NO GREENS IN THE QUICHE — MAKE THEM A SIDE SALAD INSTEAD ===

Mixed greens and spinach used to live in this recipe (mixed greens primary, spinach secondary). Both removed and moved to clashing. In-quiche greens don't do much for the flavor — the cheese + mushroom + nutmeg + parsley base is already the flavor structure, and greens folded into the custard are mostly filler that doesn't contribute much beyond visual color.

BETTER PATH: if you want greens with the quiche, make them a SIDE SALAD instead. A simple dressed side salad (mixed greens or spinach with a light vinaigrette — see basic-red-vinaigrette or cream-vinaigrette) alongside the quiche is a natural and classical pairing. The greens do their job better on the plate next to the quiche than folded into it.

=== MILK VS CREAM — BOTH WORK, DIFFERENT REGISTERS ===

- MILK: lighter custard, cleaner egg flavor.
- HEAVY CREAM: richer custard, more classical french quiche register. If you want the maximally-french-tasting version, use cream.
Either works. Half-and-half is a reasonable middle ground.

=== BAKE TO SET, NOT TO BROWN ALL THE WAY THROUGH ===

Center should be JUST SET — a slight jiggle in the middle is fine; the custard finishes setting as the quiche cools. Baking until the middle is fully firm-to-the-touch pushes past the sweet spot and gives you a rubbery texture at the edges (same failure mode as an overcooked frittata). 35-40 min at 375°F is the range; start checking at 35.

COOL 5-10 MIN BEFORE SLICING: not just for handling. The custard needs the rest period to finish setting from residual heat and to firm up enough to slice cleanly. Cutting immediately gives you weepy wet slices even from a properly-baked quiche.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- marcella-frittata: the italian egg-and-cheese-and-vegetables sibling. Skillet-to-oven low-heat covered set instead of pastry crust; same moisture-control rules for the vegetables that go in. Read that recipe's failure-mode notes for context on why cooked-and-dried vegetables matter.
- mushroom-leek-galette: french pastry + mushrooms, similar savory-french-pastry family. Different format (rustic folded galette vs pie-plate quiche).
- savory-pie-crust: the from-scratch pie crust recipe if you want to make it yourself rather than buy pre-made.
